Throughout his professional career, Joachim focused on economics, geopolitics, ESG and their impact on financial markets.

In Klement's view, the future of AI technology will be small, efficient, and cheap—making the business model powering centralized cloud AI structurally unprofitable.

In my regular research (behind a paywall), I have been saying for a while that I think the future of AI is not large language models (LLM), but small language models (SLM) run on local desktop computers or even mobile phones. In May, a team from Stanford University published research that compared these SLMs with the performance of LLMs run in data centres. If their results are true, then we will hardly need any data centres in the future, and the hyperscalers are wasting hundreds of billions of dollars in investments.
Seriously, if you are an investor trying to figure out where to invest in the AI hype, you need to read this paper in full. But to get you started, let me give you some highlights.
First, they ran a series of SLMs (QWEN 3, GEMMA 3, GPT-OSS, GRANITE 4.0) that can be downloaded on a local PC and compared their performance with cloud-based state-of-the-art LLMs (ChatGPT 5, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro).
They ran these SLMs on local PCs powered either by an Nvidia chip or an Apple M4 chip, as they are readily available in current high-end desktop computers (the entire study was done before Nvidia presented its AI chip for PCs, which will only accelerate the move away from datacentres to models run on desktops).
Then they traced the performance of these SLMs vs LLM between 2023 and October 2025 on both chat tasks and reasoning tasks.
The chart below shows the Win/Tie-ratio for SLMs vs LLMs in chat requests, which still make up the vast majority of requests today. As you can see, in every domain, the best SLM is able to find the same or better answers than an LLM in 90% or more of the cases, with an average across all domains of 98.6%.
Win/Tie-ratio of SLM vs. LLM in chat requests
When it comes to reasoning tasks, which are obviously more demanding, SLMs are catching up fast. On average, they provide a better or at least as good an answer as LLMs in 62.5% of the cases.
Win/Tie-ratio of SLM vs. LLM in reasoning tasks
However, in real life, the tasks for SLMs and LLMs are typically a mix of chat requests and reasoning tasks, so the third chart shows the weighted average of chat request performance and reasoning performance based on the frequency of tasks in each domain. As you can see, on average, SLMs are as good if not better than LLMs in 81.2% of the cases, with the LLMs having a significant advantage only in areas like engineering, life sciences, transportation and computer sciences.
Win/Tie-ratio of SLM vs. LLM in chat and reasoning tasks
But it’s not just accuracy. SLMs achieve this performance at energy and compute costs that are between 50% and 85% lower than for an LLM, depending on the SLM and hardware used in the computer.
What is more, SLMs are catching up rapidly in reasoning tasks. The final chart shows the performance of SLMs as a function of difficulty level and model generation for reasoning tasks alone.
In 2023, the success rate of SLMs in reasoning tasks was typically 50% or so across all five difficulty levels. By October 2025, the SLMs achieved 99% success for the easiest reasoning tasks in levels 1 and 2, 85% to 92% success in harder tasks (levels 3 and 4) and only lagged LLMs in the hardest tasks of level 5 (51.5% success rate).
Success rates of SLMs in reasoning tasks
This already means that one can replace data centres and their expensive cutting-edge semiconductor infrastructure in four out of five use cases. The research report estimates that the addressable market in the US for SLMs has grown to about $10tn or one-third of the entire US GDP of $30tn. There isn’t much left for LLMs to thrive in, and every year, their advantage over SLMs is shrinking.
There clearly are areas where LLMs are still way ahead, particularly in agentic AI applications, where SLMs currently only achieve accuracy and success rates of less than 50%. Similarly, it is difficult to run these SLMs on smartphones so far. The models that can be run on an iPhone are significantly worse than the models that can be run on a desktop PC.
But – and this is important – the models run on a desktop PC, and even more so, the ones run on a smartphone are much more energy efficient than the ones run in the cloud. The inference per Watt of these SLMs is typically seven times larger than that of LLMs. And that means that when you encounter a task that can be solved on a desktop or even a mobile device, it is cheaper to do so locally than send it to a data centre.
This has important implications for investors, in my view:
We need many fewer data centres than we think. If we can already replace 70% to 80% of the tasks that are expected to run on LLMs with SLMs, the hyperscalers have simply no revenue growth in the future that is nearly enough to justify the capex. In fact, if this research is true and this trend continues, data centres may be the worst investment in the AI space one can make right now.
While we continue to need enormous investments in semiconductors of all sorts, we do not need to invest in the most advanced Nvidia chips. The cheaper ones that run on desktop PCs will be enough. The best case for Nvidia is that it can replace its high-end data centre GPUs with its new chips for desktop PCs. What will that do to Nvidia’s margins and revenue growth going forward?
We still need LLMs for the most advanced tasks, and companies like OpenAI, Anthropic and others will be able to ‘dumb down’ their models to an SLM and sell them instead of LLMs. But given the already fierce competition from Chinese providers like QWEN or IBM’s GRANITE, the profit margins for these models will be much smaller than for LLMs. So what does that mean for the valuation of these companies in their planned IPOs and their growth trajectory?
While agentic AI is still better on LLMs, this may only be a temporary advantage, similar to what we have seen in reasoning tasks and single chat requests. If that is the case, the true winners of the AI boom will not be the providers of advanced hardware and data centres but the boring manufacturers of desktop computers like Dell and Apple.
Watching this race unfold is going to be fun, and I am increasingly convinced that many people will be badly burned because they invest in the wrong technology.

articles.content:
Dear Readers,
Every now and again the AI trade gets real. At the exact moment when Jensen Huang of Nvidia was most influential with Donald Trump (back mid 2025 to early 2026), there was something else going on in his personal life. This weekend it came out that the Nvidia CEO sent staff in an email that he had an affair and that the company’s board has opened an independent investigation into allegations that the woman is a Chinese spy. This is the transcript of the Email:
Subject: A message to our company
Body: “I owe my family and all of you an apology.
I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.
Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.
To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.
To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me.
Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.
Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company, and I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.
My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy.” - Jensen Huang, Nvidia CEO.
Jensen Huang's most significant involvement with Alice Huang (also known as Huang Le), an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, spans from mid-2024 through early 2026. This was the most critical period when China managed to obtain access to many of Nvidia’s critical GPUs and AI chips and who essentially caught up in the open-source AI race. Nvidia's board said an independent committee, assisted by outside counsel, will investigate the matter.
During the same period of the affair, Jensen Huang struck up a very close rapport with the POTUS and the spy’s (overreach) mission may have already been completed at this time. Huang has been a key voice in Washington pushing to loosen restrictions on AI chip sales to China.
While the AI trade tetters on the bring of a bear market, Nvidia’s stock was down 4% after the story broke. Despite strict U.S. export controls aimed at restricting China’s access to advanced artificial intelligence hardware (such as Nvidia's A100, H100, B200, and B300 chips). These tactics include shell companies in places like Singapore, Malaysia, the UAE and Hong Kong, among others. Chinese organizations have created a variety of mechanisms including overseas subsidiaries or shell entities in intermediary countries to lease server space equipped with top-tier Nvidia clusters.
Jensen Huang has long argued that keeping American technology in the Chinese market strengthens U.S. competitiveness and prevented China from developing their own potentially more advanced chips. Now in late 2026, we don’t know how much influence Alice Huang had on his viewpoints and opinions. His talking points could have come from in part, the highest levels of China. (I actually agree with him that the restrictions have actually helped China innovate in the sector and have been counter-productive). Jensen Huang has impacted AI policy more than any other Tech executive in the world, so that’s why this is a big deal.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned top Trump officials about Huang's relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence officials believed was a Chinese spy, The New York Times (NYT) reported Friday. In the days following, there’s been a ramp up of pressure. The Midterm “Blue Tsunami” wave and now Jensen’s spy story truly is bearish for the AI bull market. Donald Trump knew about the situation for at least a year and didn’t want it to hamper AI chip sales. The plot is like a honeypot spy movie plot, but has real ramifications for AI history and U.S. National security.
Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) promised a probe of the latest Times report and Huang’s relationships.
He went on to say via Axios, “The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I’m convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn’t corrupt. Congress will investigate and get answers,” Coons posted to X, linking in another post to the Times’ story.
From what we can tell from the investigative journalism by U.S. outlets, the woman, Alice Huang, was recruited to seek information and potentially push for Nvidia’s advanced chips to be made available in China, countering existing restrictions, the Times reported. It appears the affair led to a successful mission for China at a considerable cost to the Nvidia’s CEO personal life.
With so much concentration of power in the U.S’s approach to AI supremacy, honeypot spy stories of this nature become increasingly dangerous. Jensen Huang has long argued that restricting Nvidia's access to China risks undermining America's technological advantage and while his affairs don’t change the merits of his viewpoint, his proximity to Trump during that period is a serious cause for concern - there would be a lot that we still don’t know.
President Donald Trump backed Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Sunday:
"I think he's an honorable guy," Trump told reporters on Sunday. "I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it."
A bear market and a spy story, this is America.
At 6:00 PM ET, US stock market futures opened for the first time since Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to a "relationship" with a Chinese spy.

articles.title: How to Use Meta Muse as Your Personal AI Assistant
articles.content:
Good Morning,
This week we continue our hands-on AI guide series, by some of the most talented folk writing AI guides on Substack.
I really respect Product people in how they are adopting AI and the quality of their insights and their detailed early adoption notes. I asked to give AI Supremacy readers an easy to understand guide to Meta’s Muse.
Meta's Muse product was launched on September 8th, 2026 and is one of the most ambitious personal assistants in the world. Meta Muse is 56 days old and Muse Wonder Full is a decent model. Muse hit 10 Million downloads in its first forty days just in the U.S. and Canada.
Ship and scale products 10x faster with AI-powered playbooks, tools and community.
I also want to share some related minimalistic AI news related to our deep dive into Muse today.
A potential competitor of Meta’s Muse is Instinct. Instinct is developing a personal agent that can perform day-to-day tasks autonomously. In late September, did a surprise Series C for $1 Billion quadrupling its valuation to $10 billion driven by this trend of Personal Assistants. Learn about Instinct. It’s still in private access as its invite-only Beta continues.
Grok Bot limits: In a shocking development on November 1st, Elon Must tweeted about Grok Bot here1. What followed were sudden and arbitrary limits and throttling of SpaceXSI’s services, including Grok Bot. The Halloween surprise included weekly usage limits being unexpectedly maxed out, even if they hadn’t been using SpaceX’s agentic AI overnight. Grok Bot has been positioned as a success story and while it’s built by the incredible Cursor team, it’s not clear if SpaceX has the compute capacity. SpaceX had leased considerable compute capacity to Anthropic this year that boosted SpaceX Earnings in Neo Cloud revenue.
New Claude Limits: Anthropic will likely IPO in two weeks, recently has updated Claude Code to block requests aimed at recreating or cloning existing video games and blocking reverse-engineering tasks. Game devs report that the safeguard is overly aggressive. AI generated indie games are flooding platforms like Steam.
M&A Accelerates: AI-connectivity deal of the cycle. Marvell Technology’s $115 billion acquisition of Lumentum Holdings represents one of the largest mega-deals of the AI hardware boom. It’s a global market leader in photonics, optical communications, and industrial laser technologies. It’s a huge deal where Marvell’s will be able to push into optical connectivity for artificial intelligence data centers. Marvell benefits by monetizing the electronic and architectural side of the bandwidth bottleneck that enables them to better compete with Broadcom. Marvel’s stock is up 92% this year, where increasingly it appears like Broadcom and Marvell operate in a functional duopoly.
The AI IPO of the decade is nearly upon us.
Meanwhile Anthropic updated its S-1 filing, you can read the updated version here.
The company said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year.
It reported a $104 billion net loss during the period, where it had a loss of $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025.
Third-quarter revenue increased around 47%, a steep drop from 144% growth in Q2 and 132% in Q1, reaching $17 Billion in revenue with a net loss of $23.29 billion during its third quarter.
In the amended S-1, Anthropic said it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion.
Sid is a Product Leader at Enterprise companies. He writes The Product Channel, a newsletter that helps people get their day-to-day done faster with AI, at work and at home. He publishes AI tool 101s, each one tested on his own work, with the prompts to copy.
“An AI tinkerer. I'm obsessed with helping you get good at using AI” -Siddhartha Saladi
To get all-access to Sid’s publication it costs around $15 a month or $99 a year. If guides like this might be useful to you.
Muse is if anything the first major personal assistant designed to execute real-world tasks autonomously rather than simply responding in a turn-by-turn chat format with a very big budget. Anthropic is testing Duet that I recommend for Small businesses, entrepreneurs, freelancers and business people. Muse’s early momentum is exciting but also daunting. Many retailers, marketplaces, banks and even Amazon have pushed back and blocked it.
However, I should reiterate that Meta also launched Muse for Small Businesses. More specialized version of Muse remain fairly promising. Knowing how to use these personal assistants, getting the most out of them and any tips and ticks are generally worthwhile.
After writing about the era of personal super-intelligent agents about a month ago, I wanted to know what living with one is actually like. Sid Saladi spent a month finding out. He gave Meta's Muse real jobs, from his food log to a refund Google first refused, and wrote up what worked and where it broke.
The author picks 5 low-hanging fruit tasks and and analyzes the performance. While doing a detailed walk-through guide, recommended rule settings and more.
By , October 2026
I gave Meta’s new agent real jobs for a month. It won a $114.14 refund Google first refused, ran my food log for 15 days and applied for jobs. Here’s what it did, and where it broke.
At 6:56 p.m., Google turned down my refund. At 7:44 p.m., it approved it. My whole part, start to end, was two approvals, a password and a six-digit code.
A chatbot answers and stops. Muse, Meta’s new personal agent, takes a job and keeps working after you close the app. So, I just judged it on one question: did the job get done, and what did I still have to do myself?
Muse is a simplified version of OpenClaw or Hermes Agent. I think it’s heavily inspired by OpenClaw, but it makes the setup very, very easy for you.
For the past month, I gave Muse real jobs. I asked it to apply for jobs. I asked it to track my calories and remind me when I go over. I also asked it to manage my to-do list and even go ahead and complete tasks, which it did for me.
In this guide, I’ll show you:
The setup, with the permissions that keep you in control
5 jobs to hand Muse, from the most comfortable to the one to hand over last
The prompts to copy
Where each one broke, and the fix
The rules I’d set on day one
Cheat sheet: the 5 jobs, what Muse did and what it handed back. Made with ChatGPT
Muse is Meta’s personal AI agent. It launched on September 8 in the US and reached Canada on September 18. You can use it on the web at muse.ai, in the iPhone and Android apps, on Mac and iPad, and inside WhatsApp.
The difference from a chatbot is where it works. Each account gets its own computer in Meta’s cloud.
In Meta’s words, from How We Designed Muse: “Muse has its own computer, with a file system and a terminal, so it can write its own code.” It has a full web browser too. Because that computer keeps running, Muse can come back to you the next morning without being asked.
Muse is free with a usage limit that refreshes. The paid plans are Power at $20 a month and Maximum at $100 a month, per Meta’s subscriptions page.
Three settings matter before you give it anything real.
The safe Muse permission setup: personal accounts only, Ask for some actions, Draft on Allow, Send, trash and unsubscribe on Ask.
1. Connect your personal accounts, not your work ones. Settings → Connectors, the accounts Muse can read and act in. I connected my personal Gmail inboxes, Google Calendar and Google Tasks.
Never connect a current employer’s inbox. Meta’s own safety post says today’s setup “does not prevent Meta from accessing data when necessary to support, secure or operate the service.” A work inbox is not yours to hand over.
2. Pick your permission level. Settings → Permissions gives you two choices: “Ask for some actions” or “Always ask.” I stuck to number one, “Ask for some actions.” If you want to test the waters, I would recommend starting with “Always ask” so that you can approve each and every action. As you get more and more comfortable with the actions it’s taking and how accurately it’s taking them, you can move to number one.
Muse Settings → Permissions: connector and web access defaults set to “Ask for some actions”
3. Check the per-task permissions. Every scheduled task gets its own list of what it can do in Gmail. The safe recipe is to Draft on Allow and Send on Ask.
I’d also put “Move emails to trash” on Ask. Mine was on Allow.
As I said before, this is based on how comfortable you are. If you are not at all comfortable, I would start with “Ask” for everything, and then move more towards “Allow” as you get more comfortable playing with these.
Gmail permissions on one of my scheduled tasks: Draft on Allow, Send and Unsubscribe on Ask, Move to trash still on Allow
One more habit: give each job its own side chat. The main thread is one long conversation, and five jobs in one thread get messy fast. I tried having all the conversation in one single thread, but it soon got too crowded and complicated.
Cal AI is the viral calorie app that MyFitnessPal announced it had bought in March. Photograph your food, and it will estimate the number of calories. I wanted to see if Muse could do the same job without another subscription.
What I said: I started from one of Muse’s own suggestion cards, “Snap a pic of your meal. I’ll track every calorie.” It asked me two setup questions. After that I just sent photos and one-line notes after meals.
If you want to set this up yourself, start with my setup prompt. It gives Muse one Food Log file, your daily numbers, a morning check-in and an evening line. It also tells Muse to ask about a garbled note instead of guessing, to ask before it logs the same item twice, and to call a partial Apple Health sync partial, not zero.
What happened: I ran it for 15 days, September 13 to 27.
I logged meals on 13 of the 15 days.
It sent all 16 morning check-ins at 8:40 a.m., through September 28, and never missed one. Four of them called out a thin or missing day.
It caught 3 duplicate photos (”already logged, no change”) instead of counting them twice.
When my voice-typed notes came out garbled, it asked what I meant 3 times instead of guessing a food.
It read calories off a package label twice and a weight off a kitchen scale once.
Twice it went back and fixed older days on its own. Once it read a label and saw the pack was bigger than it had assumed. It corrected the two earlier days that pack showed up on.
On day 1 it asked me to confirm every photo. From day 2 it just logged them.
One entry from my Muse food log: I sent just a photo, and it logged the calories and updated the day’s totals. Background blurred.
The food log as a Muse Goal: “Sep 27 check-in ran incomplete (partial Apple Health sync, no meals logged); next check-in tomorrow morning”
The log drifted. It kept a spreadsheet, but after two weeks the spreadsheet had 3 rows. The rest of my meals lived in the chat. Fix: name one log file in your first message, and open it on day 2.
Apple Health synced partially on some mornings. To its credit, it said “partial” instead of reporting zero steps.
It can’t make you log. I stopped on day 14. The check-ins kept asking for meals, politely, every morning.
Corrections can take a few rounds. One spoken dessert name got attached to the wrong item, then swapped with the wrong item, then fixed.
On day 2, run my read-back prompt. It lists anything you sent that day that never reached the file, and anything logged twice, then waits for your answers. To fix a row, use my fix prompt, which shows you the before and after of each change. When you’re done with the experiment, say “stop the food log tasks,” then check the Upcoming tab.
I didn’t weigh my plates, so I can’t tell you how accurate the numbers were. No app is precise here. Cal AI’s own FAQ says: “CalAI is about 80% accurate.”
An NIH-led study presented in July tested the photo features of four apps, Cal AI included, and found that Cal AI isn’t accurate either. All four under-counted meals by about 250 to 345 calories on average (the results are preliminary). So if you just want a rough, comparative overview of how you’re eating, I think this is a good way to do it. But if you want pinpoint accuracy, this might not be the way to go.
When this is useful for you: if you pay for a calorie app mostly to log photos and see a daily total. Skip it if you’re under 18 or have a history of disordered eating. The full walkthrough is in my Cal AI alternative write-up.
So what I did was, I asked Muse to run my to-do list. I wanted it to maintain a list of to-do tasks within itself and also in Google Tasks, so that I can easily tell it to check things off when I’m done, or I can go and check things off manually. I also asked it to keep everything synced, and to categorize my tasks into four piles based on what it can do for me and what it can’t.
What to say: I didn’t keep my original message, so start with my sort prompt. It puts every item into one of four piles and saves nothing until you say the sort is right.
Then let it run every morning and evening on your list. Mine lives in Google Tasks.
What happened: It kept 4 Google Tasks lists in sync in both directions. In the first week, 7 items got done. Three items finished with almost no help from me:
A flight watch ran 7 checks and closed itself when the flight landed.
A refund chase got closed out.
A document check caught a number that didn’t match what I’d agreed to.
When something needed sending, it drafted it in my voice and marked it “not sent, just for you.” It only sent it after I said go.
The to-do Goal with its three scheduled tasks and the Sep 28 digest: “29 open tasks across 4 lists, nothing completed today, 2 overdue flagged”
Week two: zero done. I added 20 article ideas only I could write, and by the morning audit’s count the list peaked at 36 open items. Muse tracked every one, morning and night. It just couldn’t do my half.
I ignored the nudges. The morning nudge ran 13 days in a row. I answered it once.
Check anything it puts on your calendar. Slate’s reviewer asked for an event at 10 a.m. the next day, and Muse “added the event two hours and 40 minutes in the past.”
It once asked me to paste an access token into the chat. Don’t. Use Settings → Secure store.
Check the delete permission. My Google Tasks connector had “Delete tasks and lists” on Allow. Set it to Ask.
Google Tasks connector permissions: access, create and edit, and delete, all on Allow in my account
When this is useful for you: when a good part of your list is screen work: research, forms, follow-ups, chasing replies. If most of your list is things only you can do, it becomes a very polite reminder app.
To set the whole thing up, paste my setup prompt after the sort. It syncs your list with Google Tasks both ways, keeps the ideas only you can work on out of its count, and reads back calendar times before adding them. The one fix a prompt can’t make is the delete permission, so set that to Ask in the connector yourself.
The trial run and the Friday sweep are in my full Muse to-do guide.
Obviously, the biggest benefit a lot of people are posting about online is getting money back with Muse: checking subscriptions that you don’t use, things that have been incorrectly charged to you, or refunds that have not been credited. I think this is where Muse can help you the most.
Muse spotted a Google Cloud charge of about $9.54 a month, a small database I’d created one afternoon and never used. It added up the Gmail receipts to $114.14, drafted a billing case and showed me the text before filing.
What I said, once the case was in:
“Keep an eye on what Google responds, your goal is to get me the refund.”
What happened:
2:55 p.m. Case filed.
6:56 p.m. Google said no. The database billed whether I used it or not, so the charges were valid. They also asked why I hadn’t noticed the monthly statements.
7:05 p.m. Muse explained the reply in plain words and drafted a follow-up. It owned the mix-up, answered the statements question honestly, said the database had zero usage, and asked once for a courtesy refund. I said “send it,” 9 minutes after Google’s no.
7:44 p.m. Google granted “a one-time courtesy billing adjustment” and approved the refund.
That’s 4 hours and 49 minutes from filing to approval. My part was two approvals, one password and one six-digit code.
Google Cloud Support’s reply at 7:44 p.m.: “we have granted a one-time courtesy billing adjustment to waive these charges, and a refund has been approved for your account.” Name and project blurred.
It can’t get past two-factor codes on its own. My code came by text, which Muse can’t read. Its email connector filters out emailed codes on purpose, so you type them.
The first email guessed. It assumed the charge was Firebase, but it was a Cloud SQL database. Google’s explanation saved the case. Check which service is billing before it drafts anything.
Google’s own docs back them up: “If you are not using your instance, you can set its activation policy to NEVER to avoid instance charges.” An idle database keeps billing until you stop it.
When this is useful for you: for small recurring charges you’d never chase yourself, because writing the email feels like more work than the money. Then delete the thing you were paying for. Stopping it suspends the instance charges, but storage and IP addresses still bill.
To set this up, paste my refund setup prompt. It finds the leak and checks which product is billing before it drafts anything. It stops so you can type any two-factor code, checks for a reply every morning, and shows you every message before it goes out.
If they say no, my courtesy refund prompt has the structure that turned Google’s no into a yes. Change its first and fourth steps to match your case.
You can also use Muse to set up and clean up your inbox. Give this one an afternoon. On three inboxes, it took an hour and 26 minutes.
What I said:
“Clean up my inbox with me. Look at my Gmail from the last 30 days and list the newsletters and promotional senders I almost never open, with how many emails each one sent me. Tell me which ones you’d unsubscribe me from and which are worth keeping. Don’t unsubscribe, archive, delete or reply to anything yet. Just show me the list here.”
The last two sentences matter most. With them, the worst case is a bad list. Without them, the worst case is a missing email you needed.
The inbox prompt in Muse, sent at 12:03 PM, and its first reply: “Still crunching through the three inboxes”
What happened: The size was the first surprise: 6,835 emails in 30 days across my three inboxes. By its count, 4,100 of them (60%) were promotions and newsletters I never open.
Muse’s answer: 6,835 emails in the last 30 days, about 4,100 of them promo or newsletter noise, with the unsubscribe list blurred
35 senders to unsubscribe from, each with how many emails it sent and what share I’d left unread.
One sender alone sent 3,112, about 100 a day, and I hadn’t opened a single one.
It pushed back on two of its own picks. For the biggest sender, it suggested a weekly digest instead of unsubscribing. It also warned that one app on the list might mix account notices in with its promotions.
A keep list with reasons: payment and shipping notices, plus one platform’s notifications I open about 40% of the time. For those, it said to trim individual subscriptions instead.
A “your call” pile of four senders, each with a reason to keep or drop it.
It touched nothing. It ended with “Say the word and I’ll run the unsubscribes,” plus a suggested reply button: “Yes, unsubscribe all of these.” I didn’t press it.
Where it breaks:
Big inboxes are slow, and you see nothing until the end. Ask for partial results and you get “nothing partial to show yet,” and its progress message guessed 1,100 emails when there were 6,835. Start with 7 days, or one inbox, if you want an answer before lunch.
The open page never updated. The list landed at 1:29 p.m., and I only saw it when I reloaded after 4. If it looks stuck, reload, or check the phone app.
One tap away from unsubscribing the whole list. Read it first, starting with the picks it flagged itself.
It drafts replies with facts it doesn’t have. Read every draft to a stranger before you say yes. A YouTube reviewer told NPR that Muse accepted a Marketplace offer below his minimum and sent the buyer to his address without telling him. He had allowed it to share his address, but expected it to check with him first.
It can’t see what the connector hides. Per Meta’s safety post, Muse’s email connector “filters out one-time tokens, password reset links, and login magic links.” So if Muse says a code never arrived, check your inbox yourself.
Ask for a file if you want to keep it. My prompt said “show me the list here.” Next time I’d add “save it as a spreadsheet,” or the answer scrolls away in the chat.
When this is useful for you: if your inbox has more senders than you can name and you want to know where the volume comes from. Before you start: the setup

Muse is Meta’s personal AI agent. It launched on September 8 in the US and reached Canada on September 18. You can use it on the web at muse.ai, in the iPhone and Android apps, on Mac and iPad, and inside WhatsApp.

The difference from a chatbot is where it works. Each account gets its own computer in Meta’s cloud.

In Meta’s words, from How We Designed Muse: “Muse has its own computer, with a file system and a terminal, so it can write its own code.” It has a full web browser too. Because that computer keeps running, Muse can come back to you the next morning without being asked.

Muse is free with a usage limit that refreshes. The paid plans are Power at $20 a month and Maximum at $100 a month, per Meta’s subscriptions page.

Three settings matter before you give it anything real.

The safe Muse permission setup: personal accounts only, Ask for some actions, Draft on Allow, Send, trash and unsubscribe on Ask.

1. Connect your personal accounts, not your work ones. Settings → Connectors, the accounts Muse can read and act in. I connected my personal Gmail inboxes, Google Calendar and Google Tasks.

Never connect a current employer’s inbox. Meta’s own safety post says today’s setup “does not prevent Meta from accessing data when necessary to support, secure or operate the service.” A work inbox is not yours to hand over.

2. Pick your permission level. Settings → Permissions gives you two choices: “Ask for some actions” or “Always ask.” I stuck to number one, “Ask for some actions.” If you want to test the waters, I would recommend starting with “Always ask” so that you can approve each and every action. Muse Settings → Permissions: connector and web access defaults set to “Ask for some actions”

3. Check the per-task permissions. Every scheduled task gets its own list of what it can do in Gmail. The safe recipe is to Draft on Allow and Send on Ask.

I’d also put “Move emails to trash” on Ask. Mine was on Allow.

As I said before, this is based on how comfortable you are. If you are not at all comfortable, I would start with “Ask” for everything, and then move more towards “Allow” as you get more comfortable playing with these.

articles.title: Google has Succeeded in Disrupting Itself
articles.content:
Good Morning,
There are small signs beginning to appear that BigTech won’t be the same after the AI boom.
Just a little note on Alphabet’s bifurcating Earnings. Google just released maybe the most disappointing Earnings in its history. I don’t say that lightly. While its Search business declines, it’s investing into TPUs and Google Cloud successfully, finally diversifying its business model to be a bit more sustainable as a Hyperscaler incumbent.
The transition is so bumpy, you’d be hard pressed not to question the plan.
Google release Gemini 4 Carbon, their strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities.
Alphabet reported negative free cash flow (FCF) of $9.07 billion during the third quarter.
Google’s Capex rose 114% y/y to $51.4bn (below est $55.8bn). But operating cash flow fell 13% y/y to $42.3bn, far short of the $53.9bn consensus.
Capex is eating into Operating cash flow.
Google Cloud revenue doubled year-over-year, reaching $30.7 billion (up 103% YoY from Q3 2025).
Cloud operating income tripled to $11.1 billion, expanding the unit's operating margin to 36.2%.
Alphabet reported free cash flow of (negative) -$9.07 billion in Q3 2026.
Long-term debt is up +479% in a year, to $125.1B. Not counting debt off the books obviously.
Incumbents won’t survive the way we remembered them, the shift is already occurring.
There are serious concerns for Hyperscalers and their Capex to negative FCF. Capital expenditure ballooned to $51.4 billion in Q3 (+114% YoY), primarily allocated to data center expansions, server hardware, and TPU inventory buildouts. Google’s AI chips (TPUs) are going to be a great business, likely the number #2 ahead of AMD chasing Nvidia by the end of the decade.
Google’s Cash burn is not great: Massive CapEx outlays, paired with a $5.2B European Commission regulatory fine payment, resulted in a negative free cash flow of -$9.1 billion for the quarter.
Google’s FCF was essentially $7 Billion less than analysts expected. The stock will have a likely hard end to the week. . (Down 9% after hours on Oct 28).
Google Search and YouTube growth is anemic, certainly not what we’ve expected from BigTech over the last few decades. They are essentially being beaten in AI by both Anthropic and OpenAI. Where are the bright spots?
But for how many days, weeks and can they replicate it in a good cadence?
Google’s revenue is still $127.6 Billion and grew 25%, but there are structural issues now at the company. Spending big for an uncertain future: Alphabet maintained its full-year capex forecast after lifting guidance to between $195 billion and $205 billion during Q2.
TPU sales are included in Google’s Cloud Revenue, so they can pretend to be something they are not.
Post Q3 Earnings, the future of Google is now open for debate.
So many dualities in Alphabet’s Earnings. So while outbound search clicks from Google to external websites are in a state of measurable (and incredible) decline, this even as total Google search query volume remains high or continues to grow. How do you monetize zero click journeys well? It’s the beginning of the end of an era.
